key_insight: This audit found no robust racial or sex differences in pain recommendations, while variation across models and configurations was much larger.
clinical_relevance: Clinical AI fairness evaluations should test each deployed configuration because aggregate findings may obscure substantial differences in treatment recommendations.
method: Study 1 tested four open-weight LLMs on six acute-pain vignettes across race and sex, using explicit identities or name-only cues.
Identity comparisons were paired by case and sampling seed against a White male reference.
Study 2 evaluated 24 configurations of 17 models on the same vignettes and 50 clinician-written Q-Pain cases.
evidence_signal: None of 1,386 Study 2 comparisons survived false-discovery-rate correction; all pain-severity differences met equivalence bounds of ±1 point on a 0–10 scale.
watch_item: These exploratory, single-prompt, JSON-constrained results do not establish clinical fairness; opioid estimates were less precise, with Study 1 unable to exclude differences of about 20 percentage points.
paper_title: Do Large Language Models Show Racial and Sex Bias in Pain Management? A Counterfactual Audit of GPT, Claude, Gemini, Llama, DeepSeek and Qwen
